title: Social Network Analysis IS353 - Full Lecture Multiple Choice Mock Questions
description: A 270-question English multiple-choice mock quiz for Social Network Analysis IS353. It covers Lectures 1-9, with 30 questions per lecture, explanations, and Markdown-formatted question text.

result_messages.message: Review the lecture key points carefully, especially graph modeling, formulas, and algorithm assumptions.
You understand many core ideas, but still need to tighten distinctions between similar metrics and models.
Good exam readiness. Focus next on calculation speed and common traps.
Excellent. You can explain the major SNA concepts and choose methods appropriately.

questions.title: [L1-01] Graph notation
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What does a graph `G = (V, E)` represent?

options.text: `V` is the edge-weight matrix and `E` is the eigenvector matrix.
`V` is the set of communities and `E` is the set of labels.
`V` is the visualization layout and `E` is the plotting engine.
`V` is the set of nodes and `E` is the set of edges connecting pairs of nodes.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. A graph is modeled by entities as nodes and relationships as edges. This notation is the basis for all later SNA topics.

questions.title: [L1-02] Node meaning
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

In a social network model, what is usually represented by a node?

options.text: Only a shortest path between two people.
Only a numeric centrality score.
An entity such as a user, webpage, paper, product, or protein.
Only a community detection algorithm.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Nodes are the units being connected. The exact node type depends on the modeling question.

questions.title: [L1-03] Edge meaning
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What does an edge usually represent in a network?

options.text: A relationship, interaction, link, citation, friendship, purchase, or other connection.
The number of columns in the adjacency matrix.
The color chosen by Gephi for a node.
The final PageRank vector after convergence.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Edges encode the relationships being analyzed. Choosing the edge definition is a modeling decision.

questions.title: [L1-04] Directed graph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which network is naturally modeled as a directed graph?

options.text: Facebook friendship, because friendship is usually symmetric.
An undirected protein interaction network.
Twitter/X follows, because `A` following `B` does not imply `B` follows `A`.
A road intersection graph with two-way streets only.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. A directed graph is appropriate when the relation is asymmetric. Follows, citations, and emails are common examples.

questions.title: [L1-05] Undirected graph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which statement best describes an undirected graph?

options.text: The edge `{u, v}` has no direction, so the relationship is symmetric.
Every edge must have a probability attached to it.
Every node must have exactly the same degree.
Every connected component must be a clique.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. In an undirected graph, an edge between two nodes is interpreted the same in both directions.

questions.title: [L1-06] Weighted graph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is the key modeling issue in a weighted graph?

options.text: Weights always mean distance and must be minimized.
Weights remove the need to define nodes and edges.
The weight must be interpreted clearly, for example as strength, frequency, similarity, cost, or distance.
Weights always mean popularity and must be maximized.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Algorithms can interpret weights differently. A high value may mean strong relation or high cost, so the meaning must be explicit.

questions.title: [L1-07] Simple graph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is a simple graph in the usual lecture convention?

options.text: A graph with exactly one connected component.
A graph that can only be represented by an edge list.
A graph where every node has degree one.
A graph with no self-loops and at most one edge between any pair of nodes.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Simple graphs exclude repeated edges and self-loops, which simplifies degree and adjacency definitions.

questions.title: [L1-08] Multigraph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

When is a multigraph a natural model?

options.text: When every edge has no direction.
When multiple edges can exist between the same pair, such as repeated emails or flights.
When each node belongs to exactly one community.
When PageRank is computed without teleportation.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. A multigraph preserves repeated interactions instead of collapsing them into one edge.

questions.title: [L1-09] Bipartite graph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which example is naturally bipartite?

options.text: A directed cycle of webpages.
A clique of authors all collaborating with each other.
A user--item recommender graph where users connect to products they bought or rated.
A triangle among three friends.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Bipartite graphs have two node sets and edges only across the sets, not within the same set.

questions.title: [L1-10] Bipartite projection warning
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Why can one-mode projection of a bipartite graph be risky?

options.text: It changes every directed edge into a self-loop.
It can create many artificial edges and dense cliques that were not direct interactions.
It makes PageRank impossible to compute.
It always removes all triangles from the graph.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Projecting user--item data into user--user similarity may inflate density and distort structure.

questions.title: [L1-11] Walk
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is a walk?

options.text: A matrix whose rows sum to one.
A sequence of nodes where consecutive nodes are connected, and nodes may repeat.
A sequence of nodes where no node can repeat.
A maximal connected set of nodes.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Walks are more general than paths because repeated nodes are allowed.

questions.title: [L1-12] Path
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What distinguishes a path from a walk?

options.text: A path must contain every node in the graph.
A path must have length zero.
A path does not repeat nodes.
A path must be directed even in undirected graphs.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. A path is a walk with distinct nodes, which is important for shortest-path reasoning.

questions.title: [L1-13] Cycle
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is a cycle?

options.text: A community with maximum modularity.
A path-like sequence that returns to the starting node.
A set of nodes with no edges.
A directed graph with no incoming edges.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Cycles capture closed connectivity patterns such as triangles and longer loops.

questions.title: [L1-14] Connected component
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is a connected component in an undirected graph?

options.text: A group selected by random teleportation.
A set of nodes with identical PageRank values.
A list of all edges sorted by weight.
A maximal set of nodes where every pair is reachable by some path.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Components partition an undirected graph into maximal reachable parts.

questions.title: [L1-15] Strongly connected component
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

In a directed graph, what is a strongly connected component?

options.text: A subgraph whose adjacency matrix is diagonal.
A group of nodes with no incoming edges.
A set of nodes with the same out-degree.
A maximal set of nodes where every node can reach every other by following edge directions.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Direction matters for SCCs. Mutual reachability must hold using directed paths.

questions.title: [L1-16] Degree
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

For an undirected graph, what is the degree of a node?

options.text: The number of neighbors adjacent to that node.
The total number of nodes in the graph.
The number of PageRank iterations.
The number of communities in the graph.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Degree is the most local structural property of a node.

questions.title: [L1-17] In-degree
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What does in-degree count in a directed graph?

options.text: The number of incoming edges pointing to the node.
The number of outgoing edges from the node.
The number of triangles around the node.
The number of random-walk restarts.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. In-degree is often interpreted as attention, citations received, or incoming communication.

questions.title: [L1-18] Out-degree
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What does out-degree count in a directed graph?

options.text: The number of outgoing edges leaving the node.
The number of incoming edges pointing to the node.
The number of connected components.
The size of the largest community.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Out-degree captures how many targets a node points to, follows, cites, or contacts.

questions.title: [L1-19] Average degree
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

If an undirected graph has `n` nodes and `m` edges, what is the average degree?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. By the handshaking lemma, each undirected edge contributes two degree counts.

questions.title: [L1-20] Graph modeling questions
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which question should be asked when modeling a problem as a graph?

options.text: How many PageRank iterations are required before defining nodes?
Which color palette should be used before defining edges?
Which community algorithm should be chosen before collecting data?
What are nodes, what are edges, are edges directed/weighted, and what attributes exist?

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Good SNA starts with a modeling choice. Different node/edge definitions answer different questions.

questions.title: [L1-21] Social networks
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which structural pattern is common in many social networks?

options.text: Every node having exactly the same degree.
High clustering and community structure.
Only self-loops.
No hubs and no triangles.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Social networks often show triadic closure, groups, and heterogeneous degree.

questions.title: [L1-22] Information networks
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which property is typical of web or citation networks?

options.text: They are directed and often have hubs and authorities.
They cannot be represented by adjacency matrices.
They always have exactly two communities.
They must be undirected and unweighted.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Links and citations have direction, and a few nodes often receive many incoming links.

questions.title: [L1-23] Biological networks
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is a common structural intuition in biological networks?

options.text: They often have modular organization, such as functional modules.
They always have no clustering.
They are always complete graphs.
They cannot be weighted.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Biological systems frequently organize around modules such as pathways or protein complexes.

questions.title: [L1-24] Technological networks
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Why may technological networks differ from social networks?

options.text: They must have only one node type.
They are never weighted.
They cannot contain paths.
Their topology can be shaped by engineering constraints such as capacity, cost, and robustness.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Infrastructure networks are designed systems, so constraints and optimization goals influence structure.

questions.title: [L1-25] Homophily
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What does homophily mean in social networks?

options.text: Random teleportation occurs at every step.
Every path has the same length.
Similar nodes are more likely to connect.
High-degree nodes must connect to low-degree nodes.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Homophily is a major social principle behind link formation and community structure.

questions.title: [L1-26] Triadic closure
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is triadic closure?

options.text: Every node has three outgoing links.
Every graph has exactly three connected components.
All triangles must be removed before analysis.
If `A` is connected to `B` and `B` to `C`, then `A` and `C` are more likely to connect.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Triadic closure explains why friends of friends often become friends and why clustering is high.

questions.title: [L1-27] Social influence
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

What is social influence in network analysis?

options.text: A graph must be converted into a matrix before any behavior changes.
All nodes must have equal probability of activation.
Only isolated nodes can change state.
A node's behavior or state can affect neighboring nodes through network ties.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Social influence is the basis for diffusion models and adoption processes.

questions.title: [L1-28] Application mapping
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which modeling choice is best for an email communication network?

options.text: Nodes as people, directed edges as sent emails, and weights as message counts if frequency matters.
Nodes as email subjects and undirected edges as random colors.
Nodes as PageRank scores and edges as clustering coefficients.
Nodes as communities before any messages are observed.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Email has direction from sender to receiver, and repeated messages naturally become weights.

questions.title: [L1-29] Citation graph
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

In a citation network, what is a natural edge direction?

options.text: From the older paper to every future paper automatically.
From the citing paper to the cited paper.
Only between papers in the same community.
Always both directions between two papers.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. A citation is asymmetric: one paper cites another. This direction is important for prestige measures.

questions.title: [L1-30] High-level pipeline
questions.question:
**Lecture 1: Introduction to Graphs**

Which sequence best matches a network-analysis pipeline?

options.text: Choose colors, export PNG, then decide edge meaning.
Compute PageRank without any graph representation.
Run Louvain before defining nodes, then collect data.
Choose representation, build graph, compute basic stats, analyze structure, then run higher-level tasks.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. The course pipeline begins with data and modeling before centrality, communities, prediction, or diffusion.

questions.title: [L2-01] Edge list
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is an edge list?

options.text: A list of communities sorted by modularity.
A visualization layout in Gephi.
A matrix where every entry must be 1.
A representation that stores graph edges as pairs or triples such as `(u, v)` or `(u, v, w)`.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Edge lists are simple and flexible, especially for input files and sparse graphs.

questions.title: [L2-02] Weighted edge list
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

How is a weighted edge commonly represented in an edge list?

options.text: As a community label without endpoints.
As a pair `(degree, PageRank)`.
As a row of only zeros.
As a triple `(u, v, weight)`.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Weighted edge lists add a numeric attribute to each edge.

questions.title: [L2-03] Edge-list advantage
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is a key advantage of edge lists?

options.text: They give constant-time neighbor lookup without preprocessing.
They automatically compute centrality scores.
They require `O(n^2)` memory for every graph.
They are easy to store, load from CSV/logs, and use for sparse graphs.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Edge lists are often the easiest format for data ingestion.

questions.title: [L2-04] Edge-list weakness
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is a weakness of a plain edge list?

options.text: It cannot store weighted edges.
It always duplicates every node.
It cannot represent directed edges.
Checking whether a specific edge exists can be slow without hashing or conversion.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. A raw list is not optimized for random edge lookup.

questions.title: [L2-05] Adjacency list
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What does an adjacency list store?

options.text: Only the graph title.
Only the eigenvalues of the Laplacian.
For each node, the list or set of its neighbors.
Only the final clustering coefficient.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Adjacency lists support efficient neighbor iteration, which many graph algorithms need.

questions.title: [L2-06] Adjacency-list memory
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is the typical memory complexity of an adjacency list?

options.text: `O(n^2)` for every graph.
`O(1)` regardless of graph size.
`O(m^2)` for unweighted graphs only.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Adjacency lists store nodes plus incident edge references, making them compact for sparse graphs.

questions.title: [L2-07] Adjacency-list best use
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which task is especially natural with an adjacency list?

options.text: Choosing node colors automatically.
Iterating through a node's neighbors.
Reading only the upper triangular matrix.
Computing a dense eigen-decomposition by default.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Many algorithms such as BFS, DFS, clustering, and local link prediction need neighbor lists.

questions.title: [L2-08] Adjacency matrix
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What does an adjacency matrix entry `A_ij` usually mean in a directed graph?

options.text: There is an edge from node `i` to node `j`, if rows are defined as sources.
The PageRank of node `i` equals `j`.
The graph has `i + j` edges.
Node `i` and node `j` have the same community label.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. The row/column convention must be stated clearly for directed graphs.

questions.title: [L2-09] Undirected matrix
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What property does the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph have?

options.text: Every row must sum to one.
It is symmetric, so `A_ij = A_ji`.
It cannot contain zeros.
Every diagonal entry must be positive.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Undirected edges are mirrored in the adjacency matrix.

questions.title: [L2-10] Matrix memory
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Why is an adjacency matrix problematic for large sparse graphs?

options.text: It uses `O(n^2)` memory even when very few edges exist.
It cannot be used for spectral methods.
It always deletes isolated nodes.
It cannot represent edge existence.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Sparse real networks often have far fewer than `n^2` edges, so dense matrices waste memory.

questions.title: [L2-11] Matrix advantage
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

When is an adjacency matrix especially useful?

options.text: Only for writing CSV files.
For fast edge lookup and linear-algebra methods such as spectral clustering or eigenvector centrality.
Only for visualizing ForceAtlas2 layouts.
Only for graphs with no edges.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Matrix forms enable algebraic operations and constant-time edge checks.

questions.title: [L2-12] Sparse matrix
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

For a large sparse graph needing matrix operations, what representation is usually preferred?

options.text: A table containing only graph titles.
A random list of colors.
A fully dense `n x n` matrix.
A sparse matrix representation.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Sparse matrices store only nonzero entries and are much more memory-efficient.

questions.title: [L2-13] Representation choice
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which representation is usually best for graph input from logs?

options.text: Fiedler vector.
Dense adjacency matrix.
Edge list.
Final PageRank vector.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Logs naturally contain events or edges, so edge lists are convenient for input.

questions.title: [L2-14] Representation comparison
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which representation is usually best for BFS on a sparse graph?

options.text: Adjacency list.
Dense adjacency matrix only.
A histogram of degrees.
A list of community names.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. BFS repeatedly needs fast neighbor access, which adjacency lists provide.

questions.title: [L2-15] File formats
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which file type is a common graph data input format?

options.text: Only `.png` image files.
Only LaTeX `.aux` files.
Only compiled binary executables.
Edge-list `.txt`, `.tsv`, or `.csv` files.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Graph data is often stored as edge lists or graph-specific formats such as GML/GraphML.

questions.title: [L2-16] SNAP format
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

In a typical SNAP edge-list file, what do non-comment lines usually contain?

options.text: Two node ids representing an edge.
A full adjacency matrix row with all zeros.
A Gephi color palette.
A trained GNN weight matrix.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. SNAP datasets are commonly distributed as edge lists with comment lines starting with `#`.

questions.title: [L2-17] Indexing caution
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Why should node indexing be checked when loading graph data?

options.text: Datasets may use 0-based or 1-based ids, which affects matrix indexing and interpretation.
All datasets must start at node 100.
Indexing controls the font size of node labels.
Indexing determines whether PageRank is allowed.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Wrong indexing can shift labels, corrupt matrices, or create unintended nodes.

questions.title: [L2-18] NetworkX graph class
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which NetworkX class is used for an undirected graph?

options.text: `nx.PageRank()`.
`nx.GephiLayout()`.
`nx.Graph()`.
`nx.DiGraph()` only.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. `nx.Graph()` represents undirected graphs; `nx.DiGraph()` represents directed graphs.

questions.title: [L2-19] NetworkX directed class
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which NetworkX class is used for a directed graph?

options.text: `nx.MatrixOnly()`.
`nx.ModularityVector()`.
`nx.DiGraph()`.
`nx.Graph()` only for all directed graphs.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Directed graphs need a representation that preserves edge direction.

questions.title: [L2-20] NetworkX add edge
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What does `G.add_edge('A', 'B')` do in NetworkX?

options.text: It adds nodes if needed and creates an edge between them.
It creates a new Gephi project.
It computes PageRank automatically.
It deletes all existing nodes.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. NetworkX automatically adds missing endpoint nodes when an edge is added.

questions.title: [L2-21] NetworkX weighted edge
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which call naturally adds weighted edges in NetworkX?

options.text: `G.add_weighted_edges_from([('A','B',3.5)])`.
`G.remove_nodes_from([3.5])`.
`nx.draw(weight='all')`.
`G.number_of_weights()`.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. NetworkX stores edge weights as edge attributes.

questions.title: [L2-22] NetworkX node count
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which method returns the number of nodes in a NetworkX graph?

options.text: `G.number_of_nodes()`.
`G.forceatlas2()`.
`G.count_triangles_only()`.
`G.matrix_title()`.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Basic graph inspection includes node and edge counts.

questions.title: [L2-23] NetworkX neighbors
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which NetworkX operation lists neighbors of node `A`?

options.text: `list(G.neighbors('A'))`.
`G.community('A')`.
`G.teleport('A')`.
`G.compile('A')`.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Neighbor queries are central to local graph algorithms.

questions.title: [L2-24] NetworkX scale
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Why is NetworkX not always ideal for very large graphs?

options.text: It cannot read edge lists.
It cannot represent weighted graphs.
It is pure Python and may be slow or memory-heavy for million-edge production workloads.
It cannot compute degrees.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. NetworkX is excellent for learning and prototyping but not always for massive graphs.

questions.title: [L2-25] Gephi purpose
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is Gephi mainly used for in this course context?

options.text: Replacing all graph theory definitions.
Training a GCN with gradients.
Writing Ruby on Rails controllers.
Interactive graph visualization, layout, coloring, and exploratory analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Gephi helps inspect hubs, communities, and visual patterns in networks.

questions.title: [L2-26] ForceAtlas2
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is ForceAtlas2 in Gephi?

options.text: A link prediction score.
A directed graph file format.
A PageRank teleportation rule.
A force-directed layout algorithm for graph visualization.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Force-directed layouts place connected nodes closer and reveal visual clusters.

questions.title: [L2-27] Modularity in Gephi
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What does Gephi's modularity feature help identify?

options.text: The number of training epochs for a GNN.
The row convention of every matrix automatically.
The exact shortest path between every pair only.
Communities or clusters that can be colored by modularity class.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Gephi often uses modularity classes to color detected communities.

questions.title: [L2-28] PyTorch Geometric
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

What is PyTorch Geometric mainly used for?

options.text: Only drawing static graph images.
Only reading Gephi `.gexf` files.
Building and training graph neural network models.
Only computing handshaking lemma values.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. PyTorch Geometric supports deep learning on graph-structured data.

questions.title: [L2-29] Data cleaning
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which preprocessing issue matters when constructing a graph?

options.text: Forcing every graph to be complete.
Handling duplicate edges, self-loops, missing values, and directedness consistently.
Choosing centrality before defining nodes.
Making all weights negative.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Graph construction choices affect every later metric and model.

questions.title: [L2-30] Tool choice
questions.question:
**Lecture 2: Network Representation & Tools**

Which tool choice is most reasonable for a small homework graph calculation?

options.text: NetworkX for computation and optional simple visualization.
Only a dense matrix for a graph with millions of nodes.
A distributed GNN framework before defining the graph.
Only Gephi, because formulas cannot be computed elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. NetworkX is practical for small to medium graph analysis and teaching examples.

questions.title: [L3-01] Degree sequence
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is a degree sequence?

options.text: The list of node degrees, usually written as `(k1, k2, ..., kn)`.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. It summarizes local connectivity across all nodes.

questions.title: [L3-02] Handshaking lemma
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What does the handshaking lemma state for undirected graphs?

options.text: The sum of all node degrees equals `2m`.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Each undirected edge contributes one degree count to each endpoint.

questions.title: [L3-03] Directed degree sums
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What equality holds for directed graphs?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
The total in-degree equals the total out-degree equals `m`.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Every directed edge contributes one outgoing count and one incoming count.

questions.title: [L3-04] Degree distribution
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is `P(k)`?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
The fraction or probability that a randomly chosen node has degree `k`.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Degree distribution is a global structural summary.

questions.title: [L3-05] Heavy tail
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What does a heavy-tailed degree distribution imply?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
Many nodes have low degree while a small number of hubs have very high degree.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. This pattern is common in social, web, and citation networks.

questions.title: [L3-06] Power law
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Which formula represents an approximate power law?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
`P(k) proportional to k^{-gamma}`.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. A power law is one possible heavy-tailed model.

questions.title: [L3-07] Log-log plot
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why use a log-log plot for degree distribution?

options.text: It compresses wide ranges and can reveal approximate tail behavior.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. A straight line on a log-log plot suggests but does not prove a power law.

questions.title: [L3-08] Power-law caution
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is a correct caution about power laws?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
A visually straight log-log plot is not enough to prove a true power law.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Fitting power laws requires care and statistical comparison.

questions.title: [L3-09] Distance
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is graph distance `d(u, v)`?

options.text: The length of the shortest path between `u` and `v`.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Distance underlies closeness, diffusion speed, and path analysis.

questions.title: [L3-10] Unreachable nodes
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is the distance between unreachable nodes?

options.text: It is treated as infinity or handled only over connected pairs.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Disconnected graphs require careful treatment of distances.

questions.title: [L3-11] Weighted distance
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

In a weighted graph where weights are costs, how is path length computed?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
By summing edge costs along the path.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. The meaning of weights determines shortest-path interpretation.

questions.title: [L3-12] Average shortest path
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What does average shortest path length measure?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
How many steps are needed on average to travel between node pairs.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. It captures global reachability and potential diffusion speed.

questions.title: [L3-13] Local clustering
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What does local clustering coefficient measure?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
How connected a node's neighbors are to each other.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. It captures triadic closure around a node.

questions.title: [L3-14] Clustering formula
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Which expression is local clustering for node `v`?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. `T_v` counts triangles containing `v`.

questions.title: [L3-15] Clustering zero case
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why is local clustering often set to 0 for `k_v < 2`?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
There are not enough neighbors to form a triangle.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. A node needs at least two neighbors for neighbor-neighbor closure.

questions.title: [L3-16] Transitivity
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is graph transitivity?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
`3 * number of triangles / number of connected triples`.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Transitivity is a global clustering definition.

questions.title: [L3-17] Average local clustering
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is average local clustering?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
The average of `C_v` over nodes.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. It can differ from transitivity in heterogeneous graphs.

questions.title: [L3-18] ER model
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What defines an Erdős-Rényi `G(n, p)` graph?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
Each possible edge appears independently with probability `p`.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. ER is a baseline random graph model.

questions.title: [L3-19] ER expected degree
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What is the expected degree in `G(n, p)`?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Each node has `n-1` possible neighbors, each present with probability `p`.

questions.title: [L3-20] ER clustering
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What clustering behavior is typical of ER graphs?

options.text: Low clustering, approximately `p`.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. ER does not naturally reproduce high clustering in social networks.

questions.title: [L3-21] ER hubs
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why does ER fail to model many real hubs?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
Its degree distribution is not strongly heavy-tailed.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Real networks often have hubs that ER does not generate naturally.

questions.title: [L3-22] Null model
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

How is ER often used in network analysis?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
As a null baseline for comparison with real networks.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. If a real graph has much higher clustering than ER, that structure is meaningful.

questions.title: [L3-23] Small-world
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What are two key properties of small-world networks?

options.text: Short average path length and high clustering.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Small-world networks combine global reachability with local cohesion.

questions.title: [L3-24] Small-world examples
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Which is a classic small-world example category?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
Actor collaboration or social friendship networks.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Such networks often have short paths and clustered groups.

questions.title: [L3-25] Clustering vs degree
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why is clustering not the same as degree?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
Degree counts neighbors; clustering counts how connected those neighbors are.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. A high-degree node can still have low clustering.

questions.title: [L3-26] Hubs
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why do hubs matter structurally?

options.text: They can reduce path lengths and accelerate diffusion.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. High-degree hubs often shape reachability and spreading.

questions.title: [L3-27] Connected components
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why inspect connected components before path metrics?

options.text: Shortest-path metrics may be undefined across disconnected components.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Distances across components are infinite.

questions.title: [L3-28] Degree heterogeneity
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

What does degree heterogeneity mean?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
Nodes have very different degrees rather than a uniform degree pattern.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. It is a hallmark of many real networks.

questions.title: [L3-29] Sampling bias
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Why can sampling bias affect observed network structure?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
Missing nodes or edges can distort degree distribution, clustering, and components.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Observed graphs are often incomplete samples.

questions.title: [L3-30] Structure summary
questions.question:
**Lecture 3: Network Properties & Structure**

Which set best summarizes Lecture 3 structure analysis?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
Degree distribution, paths, clustering, random graph baseline, and small-world property.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. These are the major structure measurements in the lecture.

questions.title: [L4-01] Centrality idea
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What does centrality try to quantify?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
How important, influential, accessible, or central a node is under a chosen definition.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Centrality depends on the task and interpretation.

questions.title: [L4-02] No universal centrality
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which statement about centrality is correct?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
There is no single best centrality measure for all applications.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Different measures capture popularity, reachability, brokerage, or prestige.

questions.title: [L4-03] Degree centrality
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What does degree centrality capture?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
Local popularity or immediate activity.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. It counts direct neighbors and ignores neighbor importance.

questions.title: [L4-04] In-degree centrality
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

In a citation network, what can high in-degree centrality mean?

options.text: A paper is cited by many other papers.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Incoming links often indicate attention or prestige.

questions.title: [L4-05] Out-degree centrality
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

In a follower or citation graph, what does out-degree count?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
How many accounts or papers the node points to.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Out-degree measures outgoing activity.

questions.title: [L4-06] Closeness
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What does closeness centrality measure?

options.text: How quickly a node can reach other nodes through shortest paths.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Closeness is based on total distance to others.

questions.title: [L4-07] Harmonic closeness
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Why use harmonic closeness in disconnected graphs?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It handles unreachable nodes by summing reciprocal distances over reachable nodes.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. Standard closeness has problems with infinite distances.

questions.title: [L4-08] Betweenness
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What does betweenness centrality measure?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
How often a node lies on shortest paths between other node pairs.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. It captures brokerage and bridge positions.

questions.title: [L4-09] Betweenness bridge
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which node usually has high betweenness?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
A node connecting two otherwise separate groups.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Bridges lie on many shortest paths.

questions.title: [L4-10] Betweenness cost
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Why can betweenness be computationally expensive?

options.text: It depends on shortest paths between many source-target pairs.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Computing all-pairs shortest-path contributions can be costly.

questions.title: [L4-11] Eigenvector centrality
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What is the intuition behind eigenvector centrality?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
A node is important if it connects to other important nodes.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. It recursively defines prestige through neighbors.

questions.title: [L4-12] Eigenvector equation
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which equation represents eigenvector centrality?

options.text: `A x = lambda x`.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. The centrality vector is an eigenvector of the adjacency matrix.

questions.title: [L4-13] Power iteration
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What is power iteration used for?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
Repeatedly multiplying and normalizing to approximate a dominant eigenvector.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. It is a common method for eigenvector centrality and PageRank-like computations.

questions.title: [L4-14] Eigenvector limitation
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What is a limitation of eigenvector centrality on real directed graphs?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
Sinks and disconnected parts can make scores unstable or degenerate.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. PageRank modifies the idea to handle web-like graphs.

questions.title: [L4-15] PageRank motivation
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Why was PageRank introduced?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
To rank nodes in directed graphs while handling dead ends and spider traps.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. It improves on raw eigenvector centrality for web graphs.

questions.title: [L4-16] Random surfer
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What is the PageRank random surfer model?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
A user follows links with probability `alpha` and teleports with probability `1-alpha`.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. The stationary visit probability becomes the PageRank score.

questions.title: [L4-17] PageRank equation
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which equation is PageRank?

options.text: `r = alpha M r + (1 - alpha) v`.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. `M` is stochastic and `v` is the teleportation distribution.

questions.title: [L4-18] Damping factor
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What does the damping factor `alpha` represent?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
The probability of following an outgoing link instead of teleporting.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Typical values are around 0.85, but exams may provide a value.

questions.title: [L4-19] Teleportation
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What problem does teleportation solve?

options.text: It prevents rank from being trapped or lost and helps guarantee convergence.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Teleportation handles both spider traps and disconnected structure.

questions.title: [L4-20] Dangling node
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What is a dangling node in PageRank?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
A node with no outgoing links.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. It must redistribute rank, often uniformly, to avoid rank leakage.

questions.title: [L4-21] Spider trap
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What is a spider trap?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
A closed subgraph that absorbs random-walk probability without teleportation.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Teleportation gives the walk a way to escape.

questions.title: [L4-22] Column stochastic
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

In the lecture convention, what does a column-stochastic PageRank matrix mean?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
Each source column distributes its rank across outgoing links and sums to one.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. The PageRank update uses incoming contributions from source nodes.

questions.title: [L4-23] Incoming contribution
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

In PageRank, node `i` receives rank from which nodes?

options.text: It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
Nodes `j` with edges `j -> i`, divided by `j`'s out-degree.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. A common error is dividing by the destination degree.

questions.title: [L4-24] Rank sum
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What sanity check should hold for a PageRank vector?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
The scores should sum to 1 after normalization/stochastic update.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. PageRank is a probability distribution.

questions.title: [L4-25] Personalized PageRank
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

What changes in Personalized PageRank?

options.text: The teleportation vector is biased toward a seed set or topic.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. PPR measures relevance to chosen seeds, not only global popularity.

questions.title: [L4-26] PPR application
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which is a natural application of Personalized PageRank?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
Recommendation or local search around a user or item seed.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. PPR biases random restarts toward a target context.

questions.title: [L4-27] HITS authority
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

In HITS, what is an authority?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
A node pointed to by good hubs.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **D**. Authority and hub scores reinforce each other.

questions.title: [L4-28] HITS hub
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

In HITS, what is a hub?

options.text: A node that points to good authorities.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Hubs are strong outgoing pointers to authoritative pages.

questions.title: [L4-29] Application choice
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which centrality is most suitable for finding bridge nodes between communities?

options.text: Betweenness centrality.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Betweenness captures brokerage along shortest paths.

questions.title: [L4-30] Metric choice
questions.question:
**Lecture 4: Centrality Measures incl. PageRank**

Which centrality is most suitable for global prestige in a directed web graph?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
PageRank.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. PageRank accounts for incoming links from important sources and uses teleportation.

questions.title: [L5-01] Community definition
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

What is a community in a network?

options.text: A group with many internal edges and relatively few edges to the outside.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Communities capture mesoscopic structure.

questions.title: [L5-02] Community intuition
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

Why are communities useful?

options.text: It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
They reveal groups such as friend circles, topics, teams, or functional modules.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Community detection supports summarization and interpretation.

questions.title: [L5-03] Internal edge
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

What is an internal edge of a community?

options.text: An edge whose endpoints are both inside the community.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Internal density is central to community quality.

questions.title: [L5-04] External edge
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

What is an external or cut edge relative to a community?

options.text: An edge connecting a node inside the community to a node outside it.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Good communities tend to have fewer outgoing edges.

questions.title: [L5-05] Modularity purpose
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

What does modularity measure?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
How much observed internal connectivity exceeds a degree-preserving random expectation.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **C**. Modularity compares a partition against a null model.

questions.title: [L5-06] Modularity simplified
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

In `Q = sum_C [m_C/m - (K_C/2m)^2]`, what is `m_C`?

options.text: It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
The number of edges inside community `C`.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **B**. `m_C` is the observed internal edge count.

questions.title: [L5-07] Community degree sum
questions.question:
**Lecture 5: Community Detection**

In modularity, what is `K_C`?

options.text: The sum of degrees of nodes in community `C`.
It is only a visualization color and has no graph meaning.
It requires deleting all edges before analysis.
It means every node must have the same PageRank score.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. `K_C` determines expected internal edges under the null model.

Missing data always increases every centrality score.
Centrality can only be calculated on complete graphs.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Degree, betweenness, closeness, PageRank, and eigenvector scores can all shift under missing observations.

questions.title: [L9-18] Temporal sampling
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Why does the time window matter when collecting network data?

options.text: Edges and interactions can appear or disappear over time, so different windows can imply different structures.
Time windows only affect node colors.
Longer windows always remove all sampling bias.
Temporal data cannot be represented as a graph.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. A static graph can hide ordering, bursts, seasonality, and causality issues.

questions.title: [L9-19] Static aggregation risk
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

What is a risk of aggregating temporal interactions into one static graph?

options.text: It may create paths that never existed in chronological order.
It always removes all edges.
It makes every edge undirected by mathematical necessity.
It prevents any visualization.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Temporal ordering matters for diffusion, reachability, and causal interpretations.

questions.title: [L9-20] Reproducibility
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Which practice improves reproducibility in network analysis?

options.text: Document node and edge definitions, collection window, filters, sampling method, and preprocessing steps.
Hide all data decisions so results cannot be questioned.
Report only the final visualization.
Avoid naming the algorithm used.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Network results are highly sensitive to modeling and data-collection choices.

questions.title: [L9-21] Privacy risk
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Why is network data often privacy-sensitive even after removing names?

options.text: Relationship patterns can re-identify people or reveal sensitive connections.
Anonymous IDs make all analysis impossible.
Privacy applies only to text data, not graphs.
Edges never contain personal information.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Network structure itself can be identifying, especially when combined with outside information.

questions.title: [L9-22] Anonymization
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Which statement about anonymizing graph data is most accurate?

options.text: Removing names helps, but structural uniqueness can still allow re-identification.
Replacing names with numbers guarantees perfect privacy.
Anonymization always preserves every centrality value exactly.
Only weighted graphs need anonymization.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Graph anonymization is hard because positions and neighborhoods can be distinctive.

questions.title: [L9-23] Informed consent
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Why is informed consent difficult in social network data?

options.text: One person's data can expose relationships involving other people who did not directly consent.
Consent is never relevant to online data.
Consent only applies to graphs with fewer than ten nodes.
Edges are mathematical objects and cannot involve people.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Network data is relational, so privacy and consent can extend beyond the sampled individual.

questions.title: [L9-24] Public data ethics
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Which is the best ethical stance toward public online network data?

options.text: Public accessibility does not automatically remove privacy, harm, consent, or context concerns.
If data is public, any analysis and disclosure is always ethical.
Only private messages can create ethical concerns.
Ethics matters only after PageRank is computed.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Researchers must consider context, expectations, potential harm, and platform terms.

questions.title: [L9-25] Algorithmic fairness
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

How can network algorithms create fairness concerns?

options.text: They may amplify existing visibility, popularity, or sampling bias.
They always treat every node identically regardless of graph position.
Fairness is unrelated to recommendations or rankings.
Only visual layouts can be unfair.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Centrality, ranking, recommendation, and diffusion systems can reinforce unequal exposure.

questions.title: [L9-26] Influence ethics
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

What is an ethical risk of influence maximization?

options.text: It can be used to manipulate behavior, spread misinformation, or target vulnerable groups.
It cannot affect real people because it is only a graph algorithm.
It always prevents harmful diffusion.
It removes the need to evaluate campaign goals.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Methods that maximize spread should be evaluated with purpose, consent, and harm in mind.

questions.title: [L9-27] Community labeling
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Why should analysts be careful when labeling detected communities?

options.text: Algorithmic clusters are structural patterns, not automatically meaningful social identities.
Community detection always reveals true personal beliefs.
Labels cannot influence interpretation.
All communities are cliques by definition.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Labels can stigmatize or mislead if structural groups are overinterpreted.

questions.title: [L9-28] Robustness experiment
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Which setup best compares random failure and targeted attack?

options.text: Remove the same fraction of nodes under each strategy and track metrics such as largest component size.
Use different graphs for each strategy and compare only node colors.
Add more nodes during targeted attack but remove edges during random failure.
Compare algorithms without defining what was removed.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. A controlled experiment changes the removal strategy while keeping the graph and removal fraction comparable.

questions.title: [L9-29] Reporting uncertainty
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Why should a network analysis report uncertainty or limitations?

options.text: Modeling choices, missing data, sampling bias, and algorithm assumptions can change conclusions.
Limitations make the graph invalid by definition.
Uncertainty is only relevant in non-network statistics.
Reports should hide assumptions to appear objective.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Transparent limitations help readers judge how far the results can be trusted.

questions.title: [L9-30] Responsible SNA workflow
questions.question:
**Lecture 9: Network Robustness, Sampling & Ethics**

Which workflow is most responsible for an SNA project?

options.text: Define nodes and edges, document collection limits, validate assumptions, analyze robustness, and consider ethical risks.
Start with the most colorful layout and choose the research question afterward.
Ignore missing data if the graph is visually dense.
Publish all raw relational data because graphs are not personal data.

questions.explanation: Correct answer: **A**. Responsible SNA combines technical validity with careful interpretation and ethical judgment.
